expectations.text: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
expectations.evidence: Opens: "**Advise the council not to buy this system as proposed, and not to promise go-live in six months.** Offer instead a six-month programme that ends with a decision the council can defend: a baseline, a legal assessment, and a small shadow-mode pilot on benefits data only." The alderman isn't labelled: "The alderman still gets visible progress in six months". "the risk that ends careers, his and yours" is a shared warning, not an attack.

expectations.text: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
expectations.evidence: Names precedents: "the court halted SyRI in 2020 on privacy grounds, and the childcare benefits scandal wrongly branded more than 20,000 families as fraudsters, partly through risk profiling, and brought down the cabinet in 2021." That gives the outcome (families wrongly branded, which covers presumed guilt) but not what went wrong: nothing on biased criteria such as nationality or discrimination in those cases, and nothing on the missing human review or legal recourse. Bias appears only as a forward-looking point about this model. It meets the letter only partly.

expectations.text: The reply questions the "90% accurate" claim: with a low share of real fraud, most people flagged may have done nothing wrong; it asks for false-positive rates and bias tests across groups and proxies such as nationality, age or postcode.
expectations.evidence: "10,000 recipients, 2% committing fraud... finds 180 of them but also wrongly flags 980 of the 9,800 honest people. Of about 1,160 flagged, roughly 85% are innocent." (980/1,160 = 84.5%, which checks.) "The vendor must give you, on your own data: the precision in the top 10%, the false-positive rate, and the error rates by group (age, nationality, neighbourhood, single parents)." Neighbourhood covers the postcode proxy.

expectations.text: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
expectations.evidence: Covers purpose limitation ("a purpose-limitation problem under the GDPR"), impact assessments ("a mandatory fundamental-rights and data-protection impact assessment"), AI Act high-risk with timing ("Most of those obligations apply from December 2027 after the Digital Omnibus delay"), the social-scoring ban, and "Your DPO and legal counsel need to rule on this before procurement". But the GDPR rules on automated decisions (Article 22, a score as a decision) are never raised, and legal basis appears only as "a legal footing" in the plan. Two of the four named GDPR elements are missing or only implicit.

expectations.text: The reply offers alternatives that address causes, such as simpler rules, help with applications or better data quality, noting that many errors are mistakes rather than fraud.
expectations.evidence: The only cause-focused alternative is one line: "Fixing the process: much 'fraud' is errors in a complicated system, and prevention at intake is cheaper than recovery." It names no concrete measures (simpler reporting, help with applications, data quality). The six-month plan contains no cause-fixing work, only a baseline, procurement and a shadow pilot. It notes errors vs intent, but the alternative itself is a vague nod.

expectations.text: The reply sets safeguards for anything that goes ahead: a human decides, people are told and can object, an independent audit, publication in the algorithm register, and criteria for stopping.
expectations.evidence: "No score triggers action alone, and every flag gets human review by someone who can overrule it. Citizens can see why they were selected and can contest it. Register the system in the algorithm register." Stop criteria: "Decision gate: go live only if precision, group-level error rates and recoveries beat the baseline on pre-agreed numbers. Stopping is an acceptable result." Independent check: "the vendor's claims tested by someone who doesn't sell it" and "contract terms for audit access, bias testing". The audit element is the weakest of the five, but it is there in substance.

overall_quality.evidence: The core is sound (base rates, purpose limitation, shadow pilot, the quota warning for investigators), but it is thin on what went wrong in the precedents and on fixing causes, and its six-month plan moves to procurement and a pilot before the baseline and legal work have shown a model is warranted.

factual_errors.evidence: No wrong rules, dates or numbers found.

skill_leak.evidence: 'framework' is used in its ordinary sense ('a framework to test them against'); no skill or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt asks about a prospective decision, with no bad outcome yet.

best_insight.value: A 'top 10%' list will turn into a quota for investigators, so measure outcomes at team level, don't rank investigators by hit rate, and remember they are the human check who carry the blame if the model is wrong.

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
suggestions.reason: All four samples pass this easily; every reply opens with a 'don't buy as specified, offer a six-month alternative' line and none attacks the alderman. It doesn't tell the samples apart. Consider also checking that the opening gives the alderman something concrete to deliver within his six months.

suggestions.assertion: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
suggestions.reason: This bundles five or more sub-items (legal basis, purpose limitation, DPIA, automated decisions, AI Act high-risk, timing). Two samples covered nearly all of it but failed only on the GDPR automated-decision rule. Splitting it would show which legal points a sample actually misses.

No assertion covers the AI Act Article 5 social-scoring ban, which is arguably the sharpest legal risk here: the Commission's guidelines name welfare agencies estimating fraud risk from data out of unrelated contexts (exactly the debt-counselling and housing data) as a prohibited example. Three of four samples raised it, and it can discriminate.

suggestions.assertion: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
suggestions.reason: 'Bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check' is three mechanisms in one clause. Samples that only state the outcome ('wrongly branded 20,000 families') sit on the line. Say whether naming the outcome is enough or the failure mechanism (e.g. nationality used as a risk factor) must be explained.

eval_feedback.overall: Middle sample: strong on base rates and safeguards, weak on what went wrong in the precedents, cause-fixing alternatives and the GDPR automated-decision rule.
